name_or_item: Convair 990 against Convair 880-22: two extra engines and 10 ft stretch
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: 880-22 2 x CJ-805-3, 129 ft 4 in, 184,500 lb, 124 seats, GBP1.29m; 990 4 x CJ-805-21, 139 ft 5.5 in, 234,200 lb, 139 seats, GBP1.57m fully equipped. Difference +GBP280,000 = +21.7 per cent. Two extra engines plus a 10 ft fuselage plug and 50,000 lb more weight.

name_or_item: de Havilland Comet 4 against Sud Caravelle III: four engines against two at similar seating
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: Comet 4 4 x Avon 524, 81 seats, 162,000 lb, GBP1.14m; Caravelle III 2 x Avon 527, 80 seats, 99,208 lb, GBP950,000. +GBP190,000 = +20.0 per cent, but the Comet has 63 per cent more maximum weight and much greater range, so this is an upper bound on the engine effect.

name_or_item: Vickers Viscount 700D against Fokker F.27: four turboprops against two
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: Viscount 700D 4 x Dart RDa.6, 53 seats, 64,500 lb, GBP400,000; F.27 2 x Dart RDa.6, 48 seats, 37,500 lb, GBP218,000. +GBP182,000 = +83.5 per cent. Same engine type, so the difference is engine number plus size; used only after the weight adjustment in the report.

name_or_item: Lockheed Electra against Douglas DC-6B: turboprop against piston at similar seating
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: Electra 4 x Allison 501-D13, 99 seats, 116,000 lb, GBP818,000 (1959); DC-6B 4 x R-2800, 107 seats, 107,000 lb, GBP500,000 (1958). +GBP318,000 = +63.6 per cent. Best piston-to-turboprop pair found: same engine count, similar seats and weight.

name_or_item: Convair 880/990 after stripping the fuselage stretch: per extra engine
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645); Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 23 Nov 1961, pp.795-850 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1961-11-23_80)
notes: [COMPUTED] The 990's +21.7 per cent contains a 10 ft stretch. The VC10/Super VC10 pair prices a 27 ft stretch at +13.6 per cent, or 0.50 per cent per foot, so 10 ft is +5.0 per cent. The residual +15.9 per cent for two engines is +7.7 per cent per engine. An upper bound: the 990 also has a larger wing and 50,000 lb more weight, and its price is fully equipped while the 880's is basic.

name_or_item: Viscount 700D/F.27 after weight and seat adjustment: per extra engine
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: [COMPUTED] The Viscount's +83.5 per cent contains about +9.2 per cent for five seats and about +58 per cent for 72 per cent more maximum weight at the cross-section elasticities, leaving +6.3 per cent for two engines = +3.1 per cent per engine. A lower bound: maximum weight is itself largely engines and fuel, so this over-controls for the feature.

name_or_item: de Havilland Comet 4 against Bristol Britannia 320: turbojet against turboprop
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: Comet 4 4 x Avon, 81 seats, 162,000 lb, GBP1.14m; Britannia 320 4 x Proteus turboprop, 149 seats, 185,000 lb, GBP1.07m. +GBP70,000 = +6.5 per cent with 46 per cent fewer seats, or +96 per cent per seat. The wide range against the Caravelle/Electra pair is why the jet factor is given as 1.25-1.60.

name_or_item: Sud Caravelle III against Lockheed Electra: turbojet against turboprop
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: Caravelle III 2 x Avon, 80 seats, 99,208 lb, GBP950,000; Electra 4 x Allison turboprop, 99 seats, 116,000 lb, GBP818,000. Jet is +GBP132,000 = +16.1 per cent with 19 per cent fewer seats, so +43.6 per cent per seat. The jet premium is partly speed and wing sweep.

name_or_item: Boeing 707-320 against 707-120: engine mark change and long-range airframe
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: 707-120 4 x JT3C-6 11,200 lb, 179 seats, 247,000 lb, GBP1.68m; 707-320 4 x JT4A-3 15,800 lb, 189 seats, 315,000 lb, GBP1.77m. +GBP90,000 = +5.4 per cent for 41 per cent more thrust, a larger wing and an 8 ft fuselage stretch. Range is cheap in capital terms.

name_or_item: Boeing 720 against 707-120: same engines, 8 ft 4 in shorter fuselage
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: 720 4 x JT3C-7, 149 seats, 203,000 lb, GBP1.25m; 707-120 4 x JT3C-6, 179 seats, 247,000 lb, GBP1.68m. The 720 is 25.6 per cent cheaper for a shorter fuselage and 44,000 lb less weight; this is the fuselage-length term used to strip the stretch out of the Convair pair.

name_or_item: Avro 748 Series 2 against Series 1: Dart RDa.7 against RDa.6
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 23 Nov 1961, pp.795-850 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1961-11-23_80)
notes: Series 1 GBP200,000, Series 2 GBP231,000, Series E GBP260,000, all 1961 basic prices. Series 2/1 = +15.5 per cent for the more powerful Dart mark and higher weights; the Series E adds another 12.6 per cent for RDa.10s and a 6 ft stretch.

name_or_item: Super VC10 against standard VC10: 27 ft stretch, same engines
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 23 Nov 1961, pp.795-850 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1961-11-23_80)
notes: Standard VC10 4 x Conway RCo.42, 150 seats, GBP2.2m fully equipped except seats; Super VC10 GBP2.5m, stretched 27 ft, up to 212 seats. +13.6 per cent for the stretch and 60 seats. The cleanest fuselage-stretch price in the set.

name_or_item: Hawker Siddeley 125 radio and radar fit
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 23 Nov 1961, pp.795-850 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1961-11-23_80)
notes: Basic price GBP140,000; 'radar and radio would add about GBP25,000' = +17.9 per cent. Aircraft avionics are a large share of a small aircraft and a small share of a large one.

name_or_item: Boeing 747 against 707-320B: wide-body premium per seat
source_ref: Flight International, 'Airliner price index', 10 Aug 1972, p.183 (Wayback PDF 1972 - 2020.PDF)
notes: 747 USD24.0m, 366 seats assumed = USD65,600 per seat; 707-320B USD10.0m, 180 seats assumed = USD55,600 per seat. +18.0 per cent per seat. Seat counts are typical two-class figures, not printed in the price table, so mark the row weak on that account.

name_or_item: McDonnell Douglas DC-10 against 707-320B: wide-body premium per seat
source_ref: Flight International, 'Airliner price index', 10 Aug 1972, p.183 (Wayback PDF 1972 - 2020.PDF)
notes: DC-10 USD20.0m, 270 seats assumed = USD74,100 per seat against USD55,600 for the 707-320B. +33.3 per cent. Same caveat on seat counts.

name_or_item: Lockheed TriStar against 707-320B: wide-body premium per seat
source_ref: Flight International, 'Airliner price index', 10 Aug 1972, p.183 (Wayback PDF 1972 - 2020.PDF)
notes: TriStar USD20.0m, 250 seats assumed = USD80,000 per seat against USD55,600. +44.0 per cent. Same caveat on seat counts.

name_or_item: Airbus A300B against 707-320B: wide-body premium per seat
source_ref: Flight International, 'Airliner price index', 10 Aug 1972, p.183 (Wayback PDF 1972 - 2020.PDF)
notes: A300B USD17.5m, 250 seats assumed = USD70,000 per seat against USD55,600. +25.9 per cent. Same caveat on seat counts.

name_or_item: Douglas DC-6 against DC-4: pressurisation, bigger engines and more weight
source_ref: Flight International, 'Commercial Aircraft of the World', 20 Nov 1959, pp.576-620 (Internet Archive sim_flight-international_1959-11-20_76_2645)
notes: DC-4 4 x R-2000, unpressurised, GBP140,000-160,000 in 1946-47; DC-6 4 x R-2800, pressurised, GBP210,000-230,000 in 1946-47. Midpoints +GBP70,000 = +46.7 per cent. Confounded: 65 per cent more engine power and 33 per cent more weight as well as pressurisation. Used only for a 10-15 per cent pressurisation estimate.

name_or_item: Daimler Fleetline 36 ft single-deck against 33 ft double-deck chassis
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 20 Dec 1968, p.25 and 10 May 1968, p.33
notes: South Shields: 6 x 36 ft Fleetline single-deck chassis, GBP22,284 = GBP3,714 each. Manchester: Fleetline double-deck chassis GBP4,175 each. Same maker, same year, same Gardner engine family. +GBP461 = +12.4 per cent. The single-decker is 3 ft longer, which if anything understates the deck premium.

name_or_item: Bristol RELL air suspension option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 4 Nov 1966, p.64 (A. J. P. Wilding, 'Bristol RE single-deck bus chassis')
notes: List price GBP3,335 standard with leaf springs; Firestone Airide air suspension GBP206 = +6.2 per cent. Same chassis, same test, one option.

name_or_item: Bristol RELL semi-automatic transmission option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 4 Nov 1966, p.64
notes: Fluid clutch and five-speed semi-automatic transmission GBP364 on GBP3,335 = +10.9 per cent. Second independent bus case: Brighton 1965, GBP260 on GBP6,300 = +4.1 per cent.

name_or_item: Brighton double-deck bus semi-automatic transmission option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 30 Apr 1965, p.25
notes: Complete 30 ft 69/70-seat bus estimated GBP6,300; semi-automatic GBP260 extra = +4.1 per cent. Lower than the 1966 chassis figure because the base is a complete vehicle.

name_or_item: Seddon Pennine-6 Allison automatic transmission option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 1 Sep 1972, p.25
notes: Extra charge GBP480; the V8 Pennine-4 version costs GBP360 more again (GBP840) because of a larger gearbox. No base chassis price on the page, so no percentage.

name_or_item: Bristol RELL exhaust water heater and radiator shutter (saloon heating)
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 4 Nov 1966, p.64
notes: GBP135 15s on GBP3,335 = +4.1 per cent. The heater uses exhaust heat to warm the saloon; it is the bus equivalent of carriage heating.

name_or_item: Bristol RELL Gardner 6LX engine option against standard Leyland 0.600
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 4 Nov 1966, p.64
notes: Gardner 6LX adds GBP385 = +11.5 per cent; the 6HLX test engine is a further option. A make-of-engine premium, not a diesel premium.

name_or_item: Bristol RELL Clayton Dewandre automatic lubrication option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 4 Nov 1966, p.64
notes: GBP87 on GBP3,335 = +2.6 per cent. Recorded as an example of a small chassis option, not as a feature for the ladder.

name_or_item: Bedford SB power steering option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 9 Aug 1980, p.66, quoting the 1957 list
notes: Complete 41-seat coach GBP3,620; power steering GBP60 = +1.7 per cent. Power steering became standard on PSV chassis in the early 1960s, so the premium is short-lived.

name_or_item: Bedford SB two-speed axle option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 9 Aug 1980, p.66, quoting the 1957 list
notes: GBP185 on GBP3,620 = +5.1 per cent. Second case: Bedford SL1 1960, GBP95 on GBP1,143 = +8.3 per cent. Range 5-8 per cent.

name_or_item: Bedford SL1 two-speed axle option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 15 Apr 1960, p.51
notes: GBP95 on GBP1,143 = +8.3 per cent.

name_or_item: Guy Arab V double-deck chassis, 30 ft against 27 ft
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 22 Jan 1965, p.30
notes: Cardiff: 30 ft chassis GBP2,792, 27 ft GBP2,695 = +3.6 per cent for 3 ft. Body also GBP120 more for the 30 ft version (GBP3,265 against GBP3,145, +3.8 per cent).

name_or_item: Guy Arab V double-deck body, 30 ft against 27 ft
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 22 Jan 1965, p.30
notes: GBP3,265 against GBP3,145 = +3.8 per cent for 3 ft of body length.

name_or_item: Double-deck bus body as a share of the complete vehicle
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 22 Jan 1965, p.30
notes: Cardiff 30 ft: chassis GBP2,792 + body GBP3,265 = GBP6,057; body 53.9 per cent. Coventry 1964: chassis GBP3,240.45 + body GBP3,560 = GBP6,800.45; body 52.3 per cent. BUT 1955 trolleybus: body 46.9 per cent. Range 47-54 per cent.

name_or_item: Double-deck bus body share, Coventry 1964
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 31 Jul 1964, p.24
notes: 22 Fleetline chassis GBP71,290 = GBP3,240.45 each; 22 76-seat bodies GBP78,320 = GBP3,560 each; body 52.3 per cent of the complete GBP6,800.45.

name_or_item: Trolleybus body share, Glasgow BUT 9613T
source_ref: published-capital.md, row for Glasgow BUT 9613T
notes: Chassis GBP3,195 + body GBP2,821 = GBP6,016; body 46.9 per cent. The chassis includes the electrical equipment, which is why the body share is lower than a diesel bus.

name_or_item: Low-floor bus premium, Scania Axcess-ultralow
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 16 Mar 1995, p.16
notes: Wrights' chief executive said the aim was a low-floor bus no more than 5 per cent more expensive than a conventional single-decker, and 'the project has achieved that'. GBP100,000 for a 12 m 47-seat car, at least GBP10,000 cheaper than rivals.

name_or_item: Low-floor bus premium, planning norm
source_ref: ITDP BRT Standard, 'Vehicle Costs', table 20.10
notes: Low floor adds 4.5 per cent to a 40-seat mini, 4.25 per cent to a 53-seat midi, 4 per cent to a 75-seat conventional and 2 per cent to a 120-seat articulated bus. Planning norm, not a measured pair. Use 2-4.5 per cent.

name_or_item: Bus air conditioning premium, planning norm
source_ref: ITDP BRT Standard, 'Vehicle Costs', table 20.10
notes: Air conditioning adds 12.5 per cent to a mini, 12 per cent to a midi, 11.5 per cent to a conventional and 11.5 per cent to an articulated bus. Planning norm; no British measured pair found.

name_or_item: Trolleybus against motorbus
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 19 Sep 1952, p.80
notes: Two-axle 56-seat 8 ft double-deck motorbus about GBP4,200; equivalent trolleybus GBP4,800. +14.3 per cent, excluding overhead line (about GBP10,000 a mile).

name_or_item: Austin 304 forward-control against 303 normal-control 3-ton
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 May 1960, p.134, 'What Will It Cost?'
notes: Petrol chassis and cab: normal control GBP707, forward control GBP735 = +4.0 per cent.

name_or_item: Bedford 4-ton forward-control against normal-control
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 May 1960, p.134
notes: Petrol: GBP765 normal, GBP810 forward = +5.9 per cent. The largest of the clean cab pairs.

name_or_item: Bedford 5-ton forward-control against normal-control
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 May 1960, p.134
notes: Petrol: GBP840 normal, GBP853 forward = +1.5 per cent.

name_or_item: Bedford 6-ton forward-control against normal-control
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 May 1960, p.134
notes: Petrol: GBP875 normal, GBP902 forward = +3.1 per cent.

name_or_item: Bedford 7-ton forward-control against normal-control
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 May 1960, p.134
notes: Petrol: GBP1,080 normal, GBP1,002 forward = -7.2 per cent. Anomaly, probably a different specification; recorded so that it is not averaged into the cab premium.

name_or_item: Ford Thames Trader 5-ton tipper against platform chassis
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 May 1960, p.134
notes: Petrol: platform GBP845, tipper GBP885 = +4.7 per cent. Oil: GBP960 against GBP1,020 = +6.3 per cent. The 7-ton pair runs the other way (-1.5 per cent), so use 5-6 per cent.

name_or_item: Bedford forward-control 4x4 against 4-ton forward-control
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 May 1960, p.134
notes: Petrol: 4x4 GBP1,260, 4-ton 4x2 GBP810 = +55.6 per cent. Different model and likely different gross weight; upper bound only.

name_or_item: ERF 68GX automatic transmission, net of standard gearbox
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 6 Aug 1965, p.48
notes: Bristol Siddleley SRM gearbox GBP850, less standard gearbox, clutch, flywheel and change mechanism about GBP338 = GBP512 net. On a chassis of about GBP3,000 that is +17 per cent; the article gives no chassis price, so the percentage is inferred.

name_or_item: Ford R Series overdrive gearbox option
source_ref: The Commercial Motor, 31 Jul 1970, p.29
notes: Five-speed direct-drive gearbox standard, overdrive box 'as an option at no extra cost'. A negative result: by 1970 overdrive was not a priced feature on this chassis.

name_or_item: NER 1906 brake third: five corridor compartments against three corridor and two open
source_ref: NER carriage records, National Railway Museum, via forum-prices-part-1.md rows 40-41
notes: Dia. 251/1, lavatory, five 3rd compartments, corridor, 58 ft 6 in, 8 wheels: GBP1,459 10s. Dia. 308, lavatory, three corridor and two open compartments, 58 ft 6 in, 8 wheels: GBP1,389 8s 4d. +GBP70 1s 8d = +5.0 per cent. Same year, length and wheel arrangement.

name_or_item: NER 1911 corridor composite against 1910 partly open composite
source_ref: NER carriage records, National Railway Museum, via forum-prices-part-1.md rows 57-58
notes: Dia. 970 (1910), toilet + two corridor + composite + three corridor + toilet, 58 ft 6 in: GBP1,621 0s 5d. Dia. 1047 (1911), toilet + six corridor + composite + toilet, 58 ft 6 in: GBP1,600 16s 6d. The fully corridor car is 1.3 per cent cheaper: the corridor premium is not robust and is best treated as 0-5 per cent.

name_or_item: NER 1909 dining car with kitchen against 1909 composite, same length and wheels
source_ref: NER carriage records, National Railway Museum, via forum-prices-part-1.md rows 32 and 56
notes: Dia. 1266 dining car, pantry/kitchen/pantry, 52 ft 6 in, 8 wheels: GBP2,304 4s 5d. Dia. 824 composite, lavatory, 52 ft 6 in, 8 wheels: GBP1,594 14s 1d. +GBP709 10s 4d = +44.5 per cent. The best catering pair in the evidence base.

name_or_item: LMS conversion of 1,250 coaches from gas to electric lighting
source_ref: Hansard, HC Deb 11 Mar 1930, vol. 236, cc.1091-3
notes: LMS expenditure estimated at GBP287,500 for 1,250 coaches = GBP230 per coach, with a Development Act grant. GWR GBP80,000 and LNER GBP56,000 for unspecified numbers. On a 1930 coach of about GBP2,000 this is +11.5 per cent, but it is a conversion including removal of gas fittings, so a new-build electric lighting premium is lower.

name_or_item: LMS gas-to-electric lighting conversion as a percentage of a 1930 coach
source_ref: Hansard, HC Deb 11 Mar 1930, vol. 236, cc.1091-3
notes: [COMPUTED] GBP230 per coach against an assumed GBP2,000 new price for a 1930 corridor third = 11.5 per cent. The assumption is the weak part; the absolute GBP230 is measured.

name_or_item: Midland six-wheel against four-wheel bogie carriage
source_ref: Lacy and Dow, Midland Railway carriages, via forum-prices-part-1.md
notes: GBP979 against GBP820 = +19.4 per cent. Same body and order, one variable. The date is the 1870s, not a single year.

name_or_item: GWR Toplight steel against wood panelling
source_ref: Harris, GWR coaches, via forum-prices-part-1.md
notes: GBP1,500 against GBP1,200 = +25.0 per cent, c.1903-10. Steel panelling is the dearer option.

name_or_item: Highland Railway first against third class, same body and weight
source_ref: Tatlow, Highland Railway carriages, via forum-prices-part-1.md
notes: GBP517 5s against GBP290 = +78.4 per cent. Class finish, not structure: same dimensions and weight.

name_or_item: Midland clerestory against arc roof
source_ref: Lacy and Dow, Midland Railway carriages, via forum-prices-part-1.md
notes: Clerestory cost GBP25 more on about GBP1,000 = +2.6 per cent. The clerestory is the expensive option, not the arc roof.

name_or_item: Midland elliptical against clerestory roof
source_ref: Lacy and Dow, Midland Railway carriages, via forum-prices-part-1.md
notes: Elliptical roof GBP35-40 cheaper on about GBP1,000 = -3.5 to -4.0 per cent, while 12 cwt lighter. A negative premium for the later roof.

name_or_item: Complete set of new bogies
source_ref: Highland Railway carriage records, via forum-prices-part-1.md
notes: GBP33 per carriage for a complete set of new bogies in 1908. Component price only; the carriage it went under cost about GBP1,000-1,500.

name_or_item: Wallasey air brake equipment on a 1901 tramcar
source_ref: History of Wallasey, 'Wallasey Electric Tramway 1902-1918, part 1', quoting the 1901 tenders
notes: British Westinghouse: GBP11,940 for 20 cars without air brakes (GBP597 each) plus GBP1,000 for air brakes = GBP50 each, +8.4 per cent. ER&TCW GBP590 without; Blackwell GBP696 5s with. Builder spread on one specification 17.9 per cent.

name_or_item: Melbourne W class air brake equipment as an add-on
source_ref: Melbourne Tram Museum, 'Building the W class tram' (Warren Doubleday)
notes: Complete car GBP2,674; air brake equipment GBP154 = +6.1 per cent if added to a car without brakes (154/(2674-154)). Second case agreeing with Wallasey's 8.4 per cent.

name_or_item: Melbourne W class body share of complete car
source_ref: Melbourne Tram Museum, 'Building the W class tram'
notes: Body GBP1,383 including painting of GBP2,674 = 51.7 per cent.

name_or_item: Melbourne W class electrical equipment share
source_ref: Melbourne Tram Museum, 'Building the W class tram'
notes: Four-motor equipment including duty GBP880 of GBP2,674 = 32.9 per cent. Hawthorn 1915-16: equipment 44.6 per cent of body plus equipment. Range 19-45 per cent depending on what the body price includes.

name_or_item: Melbourne W class bogie share
source_ref: Melbourne Tram Museum, 'Building the W class tram'
notes: Two bogies GBP150 of GBP2,674 = 5.6 per cent. Contrast Blackpool 1950, where the special sprung bogies were 43.8 per cent: the share is a property of the bogie design, not a constant.

name_or_item: Blackpool Coronation electrical equipment share
source_ref: research-pricing-report.md section 2.4, quoting Blackpool tramway records
notes: Body GBP4,902 + electrical GBP2,503 + bogies GBP5,765 = GBP13,170; electrical 19.0 per cent, body 37.2 per cent, bogies 43.8 per cent.

name_or_item: Sydney open upper deck against glazed upper deck (conversion)
source_ref: V. C. Solomons, 'Sydney's double deck electric cars', Trolley Wire, May 1991
notes: Adding an open upper deck estimated at GBP140, glazed in at GBP180, plus GBP35 to lengthen platforms. Glazing +GBP40 = +28.6 per cent on the deck, about +6.7 per cent on a car of roughly GBP600.

name_or_item: Wallasey bogie single-deck against four-wheel double-deck car
source_ref: History of Wallasey, quoting the 1902 Dick Kerr quote
notes: Five bogie single-deck combination cars GBP585 each against GBP590 paid for four-wheel double-deckers. -0.8 per cent: deck type and bogie mounting did not separate the prices, because capacity did. A negative result.

name_or_item: Diesel against reciprocating steam machinery, 2,500 SHP single screw
source_ref: W. G. Cleghorn, 'Steam versus Diesel Machinery for Cargo Vessels', Trans. IESS 70 (1926), via D. Griffiths, 'British Marine Industry and the Diesel Engine', Northern Mariner 1997
notes: Steam reciprocating coal GBP38,000; diesel GBP68,000 = +78.9 per cent. Machinery only, not the complete ship.

name_or_item: Diesel against reciprocating steam machinery, 6,000 SHP twin screw
source_ref: Cleghorn 1926, via Griffiths 1997
notes: Steam reciprocating coal GBP85,000; diesel GBP120,000 = +41.2 per cent. The diesel premium falls as machinery grows, because the diesel's cost per SHP falls faster.

name_or_item: Geared turbine against reciprocating steam machinery, 2,500 SHP
source_ref: Cleghorn 1926, via Griffiths 1997
notes: Reciprocating coal GBP38,000; geared turbine coal GBP45,000 = +18.4 per cent. At 6,000 SHP: GBP85,000 against GBP95,000 = +11.8 per cent.

name_or_item: Doxford diesel against triple-expansion steam machinery
source_ref: A. E. Seaton, A Manual of Marine Engineering (1928), via Griffiths 1997
notes: Triple expansion GBP11,800; Doxford diesel with steam auxiliaries GBP24,800 = +110.2 per cent; with electric auxiliaries GBP27,200 = +130.5 per cent; R-W double-acting diesel GBP20,200 = +71.2 per cent. The widest diesel premium found.

name_or_item: Diesel premium as a share of a 7,500 dwt cargo ship
source_ref: Cleghorn 1926 and Fairplay 7,500 dwt reference ship
notes: [COMPUTED] Fairplay 7,500 dwt steamer at about GBP9 a ton in 1926 = GBP67,500. The Seaton diesel machinery premium of GBP13,000 is 19.3 per cent of that. Turbine premium GBP5,700 = 8.4 per cent. The calculation crosses two sources and a ship type, so mark it medium at best.

name_or_item: Duchess of Bedford: motor ship against steam ship of similar capacity
source_ref: E. C. Smith, 'The Progress of the Motor Ship', Nature, 24 Aug 1929, p.307
notes: When the contract was placed, quotations showed a motor ship of similar capacity would have cost GBP100,000 more. No base price in the note, so no percentage; on a large liner of about GBP1.5m this is roughly +7 per cent.
